item.title: JadePuffer AI Agent Ransomware Exploits Langflow CVE-2025-3248 and Targets Nacos
Kairos Extortion, North Korean PolinRider Packages, and EPS Supplier Phishing
JadePuffer AI ransomware, Kairos extortion, and North Korea’s PolinRider supply-chain malware
item.content:encoded:
North Korean Hackers Publish 108 Malicious Packages and Extensions in PolinRider Campaign — Must Read

North Korea-linked Contagious Interview actors are expanding the active PolinRider supply-chain campaign, publishing or compromising 108 malicious npm, Packagist, Go, and Chrome packages/extensions to infect developer environments. Victims should treat affected systems as compromised, rotate secrets from a clean machine, and audit repositories for hidden VS Code task execution and suspicious config-file changes.

  • North Korea-linked actors associated with the Contagious Interview campaign have published 108 unique malicious packages and web browser extensions across npm, Packagist, Go, and Google Chrome as part of the PolinRider activity.
  • Socket reported that 162 malicious release artifacts correspond to 108 unique packages and extensions, including 19 npm libraries, 10 Composer packages, 61 Go modules, and one Google Chrome extension.
  • PolinRider involves obfuscated JavaScript payloads planted in public GitHub repositories to deliver a new variant of BeaverTail malware associated with Contagious Interview.
  • As of April 11, 2026, the activity had compromised 1,951 public GitHub repositories associated with 1,047 unique owners and had merged with the TaskJacker cluster that drops malicious VS Code task files into repositories.
  • Socket said the latest payload reaches out to TRON, Aptos, and BNB Smart Chain services to fetch an encrypted second-stage payload that unpacks to DEV#POPPER RAT and OmniStealer.

JadePuffer ransomware used AI agent to automate entire attack — Must Read

Sysdig says JadePuffer is the first documented ransomware operation run end-to-end by an autonomous LLM agent, which exploited a Langflow RCE flaw, stole credentials, moved laterally, persisted, and encrypted Nacos configuration data. The case shows AI agents can now adapt during intrusions like human attackers, while also leaving new detectable patterns in generated payloads.

  • Sysdig researchers identified JadePuffer as what they believe is the first documented ransomware operation conducted entirely by a large language model agent.
  • JadePuffer gained initial access by exploiting CVE-2025-3248, an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in Langflow that was fixed on April 1, 2025.
  • The AI agent dumped Langflow's PostgreSQL database, collected host information, searched for sensitive files and environment variables, retrieved credentials, enumerated a MinIO object store, and established persistence with a cron job.
  • From the Langflow instance, the attacker pivoted to a production MySQL server running Alibaba Nacos and targeted Nacos with multiple payloads, including one exploiting CVE-2021-29441.
  • Sysdig said JadePuffer encrypted 1,342 Nacos service configuration items, dropped the original config_info and history tables, and created a README_RANSOM extortion table with a demand, Bitcoin address, and Proton Mail contact.

U.S. Government Entity Paid Kairos $1 Million in Data-Theft Extortion Case — Should Read

A likely Union County, Ohio government entity paid Kairos about $1 million after the group stole sensitive data and threatened to leak it, despite no evidence of actual file encryption. The case highlights a growing shift from traditional ransomware to pure data-theft extortion, where paying offers no real guarantee stolen files are deleted.

  • A U.S. government entity paid about $1 million to Kairos to prevent stolen files from being leaked, according to a Ransom-ISAC case study based on a leaked negotiation chat and blockchain tracing.
  • Rakesh Krishnan found no evidence that Kairos used an encryptor, locked machines, or demanded payment for a decryption key, indicating the case was data-theft extortion rather than traditional ransomware.
  • The leaked chat points to Union County, Ohio, which reported a May 2025 cyber incident and later notified 45,487 residents and staff that stolen data included Social Security numbers, financial details, fingerprints, and passport numbers.
  • The negotiation lasted about a month, with Kairos reducing its demand from $3 million to a final $1 million payment made on June 13, 2025, in roughly 9.44 bitcoin.
  • Krishnan traced the payment through wallets toward deposit addresses tied to Bybit, OKX, and BELQI, but the article notes that Kairos’s “proof of deletion” did not prove the stolen files were actually erased.

The File Format Your Gateway Forgot: EPS Macros Hidden in a Logo ZIP — Should Read

A real supplier’s DKIM-passing email delivered a logo ZIP that looked harmless but contained EPS vector files with macro-like code, exposing a blind spot in gateways that don’t deeply parse programmable file formats. The key lesson is that authenticated senders and clean first-pass scans are not enough when compromised vendors can send unusual attachment types hidden inside legitimate-looking archives.

  • A marine manufacturing company received an Italian email from a known supplier with a ZIP attachment named Logo nuovo.zip that appeared to contain new company logo materials.
  • A first-pass attachment scan marked the ZIP as clean, but deeper content analysis unpacked it and rated it CRITICAL with a 0.90 score.
  • The archive contained a brand-manual PDF and two EPS vector files that were flagged for VBA-like or macro-like strings, while the DOCX files had no macro hits and a PNG signature image was judged low risk.
  • The article explains that EPS is a programmable PostScript format that email gateways may treat like a simple image and fail to parse deeply.
  • The message passed DKIM from the supplier’s real domain but had no SPF record and no DMARC policy, and the article describes this as likely vendor email compromise.
